analysis.title: GS Goel - Conversations 19 Oct 2026
key_insights: Last week clients shifted from celebrating AI-driven growth to questioning the cost of funding it. GS frames this as a new, more complicated phase of the AI sequence, with an intense debate over both the availability and the cost of capital (Tony Pasquariello).

AI credit spreads widened to the worst levels of the year. The AI leaders-vs-laggards basket has given back all of its first-half 2026 gains. The gap between high- and low-quality assets is widening across both credit and equities, a defensive shift toward quality and balance sheet strength.

The GS credit team (Mark Wilson) puts AI-related bonds from neoclouds or issuers with frontier lab exposure at the epicentre of the funding cost debate. Triggers were scrutiny of AI funding models, CoreWeave-related commentary and debate over frontier lab economics and value capture. Mark argues this is not a collapse of the secular AI thesis and cites OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar saying 'we're still short compute'.

Friday showed 'the first real sign of panic in index protection' (Lee Coppersmith). VIX futures volume hit 3.6x normal, CBOE index put volume set an all-time record, and VIX call activity was second-highest in five years. Dealer gamma fell substantially and hedge funds cut risk.

Prime data showed US long/short net leverage down 3.2 percentage points, the largest weekly decline since Liberation Day. Global Tech saw its largest percentage net selling on record since 2016. Managers mostly added shorts rather than exiting longs, so portfolios are more defensive but not capitulating. Lee: 'the market is moving into a different volatility environment but not necessarily a more bearish one.'

Tech absorbed most of the damage (Peter Callahan). The Nasdaq had its worst week since Liberation Day, and semiconductors had their longest losing streak since 2008. Unlike July's technical momentum unwind, this decline has opened a real debate on the durability of AI growth.

Valuations have reset. Semiconductors de-rated from about 29x forward earnings this summer to 17x. The Nasdaq trades near its lowest multiple since the AI cycle began in 2023. The open question is whether expectations have fallen enough.

Louis Miller argues to 'buy the broadening'. AI beneficiaries are down about 25% from highs, but SPX ex-AI has substantially outperformed, quality factors are at new highs, and non-AI growth is attracting capital. His team favours quality, healthcare and selected international opportunities and sees rotation rather than market-wide deterioration.

Brian Garrett: US long/short net exposure is at five-year lows and sentiment has deteriorated sharply, while breadth is improving. About 350 S&P constituents rose last week and SPX ex-AI beat the benchmark by nearly 500bps. 'The next move is more dependent on earnings confirmation than anything else.'

14% of the S&P reports this week and another 44% the following week. Earnings will decide whether investors regain confidence in AI spending and returns, and whether this is a temporary growth scare or a lasting regime shift.

tension_points.bull_case: The AI mega-theme is intact (Mark Wilson), demand remains robust (OpenAI CFO: still short compute), valuations have reset (semis 17x vs 29x), positioning is at five-year lows and breadth is improving.
tension_points.bear_case: AI credit spreads are at the year's widest, AI beneficiaries are down about 25%, frontier lab economics and value capture are in question, and funding cost is rising.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Earnings over the next two weeks (14% of the S&P this week, 44% next) failing to confirm AI spending and returns would turn the growth scare into a lasting regime shift.
